scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: A skydiver falls at around two hundred kilometres an hour, then a sheet of fabric slows them to a gentle landing. How?

scenes.name: terminal
scenes.text: Falling, gravity pulls you down while air pushes up. Soon they balance, and you stop speeding up. That's terminal velocity.

scenes.name: drag
scenes.text: Air resistance, called drag, grows with your size and speed. A small body falling headfirst has little drag.

scenes.name: canopy
scenes.text: A parachute opens a huge canopy that catches a massive amount of air, creating far more drag.

scenes.name: slow
scenes.text: Gravity and drag balance again, but at a much lower speed, around twenty kilometres an hour.

scenes.name: pilot
scenes.text: A small pilot chute pulls the main canopy out first, so it opens smoothly instead of with a sudden jerk.

scenes.name: steer
scenes.text: Modern square parachutes act like wings. Pulling toggles lets jumpers steer and slow down before landing.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: More area, more drag, slower fall. Follow for more on how things really work.
